marking_schemes.question_text: When a bell is fixed on a cycle rings, then the energy conversion that takes place is: (a) gravitational potential energy to sound energy (b) kinetic energy to sound energy (c) sound energy to electrical energy (d) sound energy to mechanical energy
options: a. gravitational potential energy to sound energy
b. kinetic energy to sound energy
c. sound energy to electrical energy
d. sound energy to mechanical energy
marking_schemes.correct_answer: b. kinetic energy to sound energy
key_points: kinetic energy converts to sound energy
common_errors: confused gravitational potential energy to sound energy
wrote electrical energy to sound energy due to rote learning
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most candidates answered correctly; discourage rote learning; discuss examples leading to same energy conversions.

marking_schemes.question_text: A door lock is opened by turning the lever (handle) of length 0.2 m. If the moment of force produced is 1 Nm, then the minimum force required is: (a) 5 N (b) 10 N (c) 20 N (d) 0.2 N
common_errors: multiplied 1 Nm and 0.2 m instead of dividing
answered by guesswork
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Encourage attention to units, insist writing formula then substitution.

marking_schemes.question_text: A force 'F' moves a load from A to C as shown in the figure below. For the calculation of the work done, which of these lengths would you use as the displacement? (a) 3m (b) 4m (c) 5m (d) 7m
key_points: Displacement should be in the direction of force F
common_errors: selected height 3m instead of length of slant surface (direction of force not considered)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Reinforce that displacement should be in the direction of force.

marking_schemes.question_text: A radioactive nucleus containing 128 nucleons emits a β – particle. After β – emission the number of nucleons present in the nucleus will be: (a) 128 (b) 129 (c) 124 (d) 127
key_points: Beta emission does not change total nucleon number, a neutron splits into a proton and electron
common_errors: added 1 as atomic number increases
wrote 127 confused whether to add or subtract
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify that during beta emission a neutron splits into proton and electron, keeping total nucleon number same.

marking_schemes.question_text: Assertion (A): Ultraviolet radiations are scattered more as compared to the microwave radiations. Reason (R): Wavelength of ultraviolet radiation is more than the wavelength of microwave radiation. (a) Both A and B are true. (b) A is true but R is false. (c) A is false but R is true (d) Both A and R are false.
options: a. Both A and B are true.
b. A is true but R is false.
c. A is false but R is true
d. Both A and R are false.
marking_schemes.correct_answer: b. A is true but R is false.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (b) A is true but R is false
key_points: UV has shorter wavelength than microwave, so R is false; A is true as shorter wavelength scatters more
marking_schemes.model_answer: A is true but R is false
common_errors: selected both A and R true
selected A is false but R is true
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Use mnemonics to remember order of radiations in EM spectrum; give practice on Assertion-Reason questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: When the stem of vibrating tuning fork is pressed on a table, the tabletop starts vibrating. These vibrations are definitely an example of: (a) resonance (b) natural vibrations (c) forced vibrations (d) damped vibrations
key_points: Forced vibrations occur when a vibrating body is pressed on another surface
common_errors: confused with resonance or damped vibrations
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain difference between resonance, forced vibration and damped vibrations clearly.

marking_schemes.question_text: Which of the following is a class III lever? (a) Pair of scissors (b) Wheelbarrow (c) Crowbar (d) Human forearm
key_points: Class III lever has effort between fulcrum and load
common_errors: answered incorrectly due to unclear concept
supported correct answer with wrong diagram
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Advise students to make rough sketches to identify position of L, F and E.

marking_schemes.question_text: The specific resistance of a conductor depends on its: (a) length (b) material (c) area of cross section (d) radius
key_points: Specific resistance depends only on material of conductor
common_errors: confused specific resistance with factors affecting resistance
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Use analogy of density (depends on material) to teach specific resistance.

marking_schemes.question_text: Identify the option that displays the correct wiring with correct colour code (options a-d showing appliance wiring diagrams with brown/blue/yellow wire labels).
options: a. Brown wire / Mains / Blue wire
b. Brown wire / Mains / Yellow wire
c. Brown wire / Mains / Blue wire (different switch position)
d. Brown wire / Mains / Yellow wire (different switch position)
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (a) [diagram with correct switch position and brown/blue wire colour code]
key_points: Correct position of switch on live (brown) wire
common_errors: could not relate colour coding with L, N, E wires
difficulty applying both switch position and wire colour conditions
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students in drawing circuit diagrams with correct position of switch, fuse, live, neutral and earth wire.

marking_schemes.question_text: The potential difference between terminals of a cell in a closed electric circuit is: (a) terminal voltage (b) electro motive force (c) voltage drop (d) none of these
key_points: Terminal voltage is p.d. across cell terminals in a closed circuit
common_errors: missed the keyword 'closed' and answered e.m.f.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain e.m.f., terminal voltage and potential drop as different potential differences across different resistors.

marking_schemes.question_text: During melting of ice at 0°C the: (a) energy is released and temperature remains constant. (b) energy is absorbed and temperature remains constant. (c) energy is released and temperature decreases. (d) energy is absorbed and temperature increases.
options: a. energy is released and temperature remains constant.
b. energy is absorbed and temperature remains constant.
c. energy is released and temperature decreases.
d. energy is absorbed and temperature increases.
marking_schemes.correct_answer: b. energy is absorbed and temperature remains constant.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (b) energy is absorbed and temperature remains constant.
key_points: During melting, latent heat is absorbed with no rise in temperature
marking_schemes.model_answer: energy is absorbed and temperature remains constant.
common_errors: applied simple logic that absorption always increases temperature
unclear latent heat concept
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify heat absorbed/released during change of phase never affects average kinetic energy but affects potential energy.

marking_schemes.question_text: Linear magnification(m) produced by a concave lens is: (a) m < 1 (b) m > 1 (c) m = 1 (d) m = 2
key_points: Concave lens always forms diminished virtual image, m<1
common_errors: not clear with mathematical symbols greater/less than
could not correlate magnification as ratio I:O
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain magnification concept in detail with practical demonstration.

marking_schemes.question_text: A radioactive element is placed in an evacuated chamber. Then the rate of radioactive decay will: (a) Decrease (b) Increase (c) Remain unchanged (d) Depend on the surrounding temperature
options: d. Depend on the surrounding temperature
key_points: Radioactivity is independent of physical and chemical changes/environment
common_errors: mistakenly associated radioactive reactions with chemical reactions influenced by physical environment
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise that radioactivity is independent of all physical and chemical changes.

marking_schemes.question_text: The graph given below shows heat energy supplied against change in temperature when no energy is lost to the surrounding. The slope of this graph will give: (a) Specific heat capacity (b) Latent heat of fusion (c) Latent heat of vaporization (d) Heat capacity
key_points: Slope of heat energy vs change in temperature graph = heat capacity
common_errors: selected options a and c
could not connect concept of slope to different situations
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Revise concept of finding physical quantities from slope of graph.

marking_schemes.question_text: A block of glass is pushed into the path of the light as shown below. Then the converging point X will: (a) Move away from the slab (b) Move towards the slab (c) Not shift (d) Move towards the left side of the lens
options: a. Move away from the slab
d. Move towards the left side of the lens
marking_schemes.correct_answer: a. Move away from the slab
key_points: Pushing glass block into path of light is similar to placing lens in water; convergence point shifts
common_errors: found question confusing, not striking depth in thinking
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Create similar critical thinking questions for regular class tests.

marking_schemes.question_text: In the following atoms, which one is a radioisotope? Give one use of this isotope. O16, C14, N14, He4
marking_schemes.scheme_text: C14 Carbon Dating or implied/ archaeology/ tracers/any other correct use.
marking_schemes.model_answer: C14 is the radioisotope; used in carbon dating.
common_errors: wrote other options like He4, O16
gave generalised use instead of specific to C14
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss uses pertaining to radiations in class.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name the class of the lever shown in the picture below (bottle opener type lever image).
key_points: Load between fulcrum and effort - Class II lever
common_errors: wrote Class I or Class III, unclear about position of fulcrum
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay emphasis on identifying position of F, L, E; avoid rote learning.

marking_schemes.question_text: Fill in the blanks: When a stone tied to a string is rotated in a horizontal plane, the tension in the string provides __________ force necessary for circular motion.
common_errors: mentioned rotational, tension force instead of centripetal
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain centripetal force concept with diagram and relevant examples.

marking_schemes.question_text: Fill in the blanks: Work done by this force at any instant is __________.
key_points: Centripetal force is perpendicular to displacement at every instant, so work is zero
common_errors: wrote constant instead of zero
wrote formula W=F×s without answer
reasoning based on net zero displacement of full circle instead of perpendicularity at each instant
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain with examples of positive, negative and zero work clearly indicating direction of force and displacement.

marking_schemes.question_text: A non uniform beam of weight 120 N pivoted at one end is shown in the diagram below. Calculate the value of F to keep the beam in equilibrium. (Distances: 0.20 m to weight's line of action from pivot at C.G. is 0.8m from pivot to F point.)
marking_schemes.scheme_text: By Pr. of moments 120 × 0.2 = F × 0.8 [Substitution in any form.] ∴ F = 120×0.2/0.8 = 24/0.8 = 30 N (Also accept F = 120×0.2/(0.8+x) N form if applicable)
marking_schemes.model_answer: By principle of moments: 120 × 0.2 = F × 0.8, so F = 24/0.8 = 30 N
common_errors: considered anticlockwise moment as F×0.6 instead of F×0.8
confused fulcrum with C.G.
could not interpret diagram correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give rigorous practice on non-uniform distribution of mass; encourage students to sketch diagram themselves.

marking_schemes.question_text: Meera chose to use a block and tackle system of '9' pulleys instead of a single movable pulley to lift a heavy load. What is the advantage of using a block and tackle system over a single movable pulley?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (Block and tackle system) increases the M.A. or VR/reduces effort/multiplies force or effort/ to have MA>2 or Implied.
marking_schemes.model_answer: A block and tackle system increases the mechanical advantage/velocity ratio, reducing the effort needed to lift the load.
common_errors: mentioned convenience in changing direction of effort or use of own weight instead of MA increase
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain how VR changes with increase in number of pulleys with convenient and inconvenient direction.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why should she connect more number of pulleys in the upper fixed block?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: To minimise the energy loss (in lifting the movable part of the machine)/ increase the efficiency/ change the effort to a convenient or downward direction/decrease the weight of the lower block/ or implied.
marking_schemes.model_answer: More pulleys in the upper fixed block reduce the weight of the lower movable block, minimising energy loss and increasing efficiency, while keeping the effort direction convenient.
common_errors: repeated same answer as part (a), failed to understand comparison was between number of pulleys in fixed vs movable block
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Encourage students to grasp formula linking efficiency with number of pulleys in the block and tackle system.

marking_schemes.question_text: Sumit does 600 J of work in 10 min and Amit does 300 J of work in 20 min. Calculate the ratio of the powers delivered by them.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: P1: P2 = 600/(10×60) : 300/(20×60) / can be explained in words the mathematical process. P1: P2 = 4:1 /Explained in word./if 1:4 is written then P2:P1 must be mentioned.
common_errors: unable to convert ratio to simplest form
multiplied instead of dividing
gave ratio in reversed order 1:4 instead of 4:1
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Reiterate that 'compare' questions must be answered in ratio form x:y, in same order as given.

marking_schemes.question_text: 5 bulbs are connected in series in a room. One bulb is fused. It is removed and remaining 4 bulbs are again connected in series to the same circuit. What will be the effect on Resistance? (Increases, Decreases, Remain Same)
key_points: Fewer bulbs in series means lower total resistance
common_errors: used variety of words instead of increases/decreases/remains same
assumed answer without logical deduction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Encourage students to represent circuits diagrammatically when in doubt.

marking_schemes.question_text: 5 bulbs are connected in series in a room. One bulb is fused. It is removed and remaining 4 bulbs are again connected in series to the same circuit. What will be the effect on Intensity of light? (Increases, Decreases, Remain Same)
key_points: Decreased resistance leads to increased current, hence increased intensity
common_errors: unclear about relation between resistance, current and intensity/brightness
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise that for same P.D., resistance and current are inversely proportional, and current and intensity are directly proportional.

marking_schemes.question_text: Rohan conducted experiments on echo in different media. He observed that a minimum distance of 'x' meters is required for the echo to be heard in oxygen and 'y' meters in benzene. Compare 'x' and 'y'. Justify your answer. Speed of sound in oxygen: 340 ms-1, Speed of sound in benzene: 200 ms-1
marking_schemes.scheme_text: x>y. Speed of sound in oxygen> speed of sound in benzene/or implied. Or x:y = (340×0.1)/2 : (200×0.1)/2 [time taken is 0.1 s]. x:y = 17:10
key_points: x > y since speed in oxygen is greater
using minimum time 0.1s for echo, ratio calculation gives x:y=17:10
marking_schemes.model_answer: x:y = (340×0.1)/2 : (200×0.1)/2 = 17:10, since minimum echo time is 0.1s and speed of sound in oxygen is greater than in benzene, x > y.
common_errors: could not write final answer in ratio form
randomly divided 340 by 200 without justification
did not use minimum echo time of 0.1s
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Reiterate 'compare' questions must be answered in ratio form; give rigorous practice in numericals.

marking_schemes.question_text: In a reading glass what is the position of the object with respect to the convex lens used?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Within or shorter than the focal length/between F and O/ between lens and focal plane/ accept diagram (only check for the object position) or implied.
key_points: Object placed within focal length of convex lens
marking_schemes.model_answer: The object is placed within (shorter than) the focal length of the convex lens, i.e., between the lens and its focal point.
common_errors: unable to give exact position of object
did not relate reading glass to magnifying glass, used guesswork
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate concepts in class; adequate practice of diagrams for image characteristics.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why can we not use concave lens for the same purpose (reading glass)?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (Concave lens gives upright but) diminished image/ since m<1 or implied.
key_points: Concave lens gives diminished virtual image (m<1), unsuitable for magnifying
marking_schemes.model_answer: A concave lens always forms a diminished virtual image (m<1), so it cannot magnify objects like a reading glass requires.
common_errors: related to divergent nature of lens instead of image size
failed to link with part (a)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise that both lenses form virtual images but concave lens image is diminished, convex lens image is magnified.

marking_schemes.question_text: A fuse is rated 5 A. Can it be used with a geyser rated 1540 W, 220 V. Write Yes or No. Give supporting calculations to justify your answer.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: I = P/V = 1540/220 = 7A (must). No, it cannot be used.
key_points: Since 7A > 5A rating, fuse cannot be used
marking_schemes.model_answer: I = P/V = 1540/220 = 7A. Since this exceeds the fuse rating of 5A, the fuse cannot be used with this geyser.
common_errors: misconception that fuse rating should be lower than max current to protect appliance
calculation errors, missed unit 'ampere'
lack of supporting calculation for 'cannot be used' answer
calculated R instead of I
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain that current in fuse can exceed max rating briefly without immediate melting due to resistivity and melting point properties.

marking_schemes.question_text: State two factors affecting the speed of rotation of the coil in a D.C. motor.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Directly proportional to/ Increase with the increase in: the current (through the coil); the strength of the magnetic field/magnet; the number of turns (of the coil); the area/width (of the coil). [Any two points.]
marking_schemes.model_answer: The speed of rotation of the coil in a D.C. motor increases with (any two): the current through the coil, the strength of the magnetic field, the number of turns of the coil, or the area of the coil.
common_errors: confused turns of coil with number of coils
missed 'strength of magnetic field' and just wrote 'magnet'
included incorrect additional factors
confused motor factors with generator factors
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain difference between number of coils and number of turns; ensure awareness of updated syllabus.

marking_schemes.question_text: How much heat is required to convert 500 g of ice at 0°C to water at 0°C? The latent heat of fusion of ice is 330 Jg-1.
common_errors: missing or incorrect unit
converted mass to kg but used same latent heat value
used 336 Jg-1 instead of given 330 Jg-1
calculation errors
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise use of correct data from the question and mention unit in answer.

marking_schemes.question_text: Copy and complete the nuclear reaction by filling in the blanks. 92U235 + 0n1 → 56Ba--- + ---Kr92 + 3 0n1
common_errors: got mass number of Ba as 143 instead of 141
did not account for 3 neutrons when balancing atomic number of Kr
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay emphasis on explaining how nuclear reactions are balanced.

marking_schemes.question_text: The image of a candle flame placed at a distance of 36 cm from a spherical lens, is formed on a screen placed at a distance of 72 cm from the lens. Calculate the focal length of the lens and its power.
common_errors: interchanged object and image distance
wrong sign convention
wrong lens formula
left answer as fraction
did not convert focal length to metres for power
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain sign convention clearly; insist applying sign convention at substitution stage.

marking_schemes.question_text: Below is an incomplete table showing the arrangement of electromagnetic spectrum in the increasing order of their wavelength: Gamma ray, X-ray, UV rays, Visible rays, Infrared, A, Radio waves. Identify the radiation A.
key_points: A lies between infrared and radio waves in increasing wavelength order = microwaves
common_errors: applied guesswork
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give practice of similar questions regularly.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name the radiation used to detect fracture in bones.
key_points: X-rays are used to detect bone fractures
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Almost all candidates identified this correctly.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name one property common to both A and Radio waves.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Travel with speed 3 × 10^8 ms-1 in vacuum and air or do not require a medium to travel or can be reflected or can be refracted/ Scatters least. (Any one correct property.)
key_points: Common property between microwaves and radio waves - any one of: same speed in vacuum, no medium required, can be reflected/refracted, scatters least
marking_schemes.model_answer: Both travel with speed 3×10^8 ms⁻¹ in vacuum and do not require a medium to travel.
common_errors: gave vague answers like 'long or short wavelength'
wrote 'uses' instead of 'properties'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain common as well as distinguishing properties of all EM spectrum radiations.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why do we use red colour as a danger signal on the top of a skyscraper?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (Red colour has) longer wavelength/ (and therefore they) scatter the least/can be seen from a longer distance/travel long distance through the fog.
key_points: Red has longest wavelength among visible colours
scatters the least, hence visible from far/through fog
marking_schemes.model_answer: Red light has the longest wavelength among visible colours, so it scatters the least and can be seen clearly from a long distance, even through fog.
common_errors: related longer wavelength to refraction instead of scattering
gave general statement without proper reasoning
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide clarity on concepts of scattering, deviation, refraction through detailed discussion.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram below shows the path of a blue ray through the prism with an angle of 133° marked. Calculate the critical angle of the material of the prism for blue colour.
common_errors: confused, could not show proper working
gave angle as 47° or 133°
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Provide rigorous practice in ray diagrams pertaining to TIR/critical angle; emphasise angle of incidence measured from normal.

marking_schemes.question_text: What is the measure of the angle of this prism (A)?
common_errors: erroneously wrote 90° or 47°
assumed isosceles triangle and wrote 45°
calculated all angles but did not identify which was prism angle
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain geometrical concepts involved properly; encourage calculating each angle using laws of refraction and geometry.

marking_schemes.question_text: Which colour should replace the blue ray, for the ray to undergo Total Internal Reflection?
key_points: Violet/indigo has smaller critical angle than blue, so it would undergo TIR at same angle
common_errors: mentioned any colour without concept clarity
many answered 'red' incorrectly showing lack of understanding of relation between critical angle and wavelength
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain relation between critical angle and wavelength for VIBGYOR colours.

marking_schemes.question_text: Refractive index of glass with respect to water is 9/8. Find the refractive index of water with respect to glass.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most candidates answered correctly in fractional form.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name the principle used to find the value in part (a).
common_errors: wrote law of refraction/reflection/Snell's law instead of principle of reversibility
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain difference between 'Name' and 'State' type questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: If we change the temperature of water, then will the ratio 9/8 remain the same? Write Yes or No.
key_points: Refractive index depends on temperature/density; ratio will change (decrease)
common_errors: answered without conceptual understanding
could not express clearly as Yes/No
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students to answer Yes/No questions with clear response.

marking_schemes.question_text: Light travels a distance of '10x' units in time 't1' in vacuum and it travels a distance of 'x' units in time 't2' in a denser medium. 'Light covers a distance of '20x' units in time 't1' in diamond.' State true or false.
key_points: Light travels fastest in vacuum, so it cannot cover more distance in diamond in same time
common_errors: answered 'true' unable to connect fact that light travels fastest in vacuum
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain that light travels fastest in vacuum, covering maximum distance compared to any other medium.

marking_schemes.question_text: Calculate the refractive index of the medium in terms of 't1' and 't2'.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: μ = (10x/t1)/(x/t2) or μ = (10x/t1)×(t2/x) — 1(any one velocity is calculated.) μ = 10t2/t1
key_points: μ = velocity in vacuum/velocity in medium
common_errors: calculated velocity separately but made errors finding refractive index
used 20x instead of separately calculating both media velocities
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Guide students on finding refractive index from velocities; provide practice of application-based questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: A monochromatic ray of light is incident on an equilateral prism placed at minimum deviation position with an angle of incidence 45° as shown in the diagram. Copy the diagram and complete the path of the ray PQ.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Showing refracted ray parallel to the base. Completing the path of emergent ray bending away from the normal. Avoid missing arrows on refracted or emergent ray.
key_points: Refracted ray parallel to base at minimum deviation
Emergent ray bends away from normal
marking_schemes.model_answer: At minimum deviation for an equilateral prism, the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to the base, and the emergent ray bends away from the normal, with angle of emergence equal to angle of incidence (45°).
common_errors: missed arrows on light ray
did not draw refracted ray parallel to base
did not mark ∠e=∠i
showed total internal reflection instead
drew dotted lines instead of continuous lines
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Regular practice of ray diagrams with arrows; explain conditions for minimum deviation.

marking_schemes.question_text: State two factors on which the angle of deviation depends.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Angle of deviation depends on: the angle of the prism; the refractive index of the medium/material of the prism; Wavelength/colour of light; the angle of incidence. (any two points, conditions apply.)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The angle of deviation depends on (any two): the angle of the prism, the refractive index of the prism material, the wavelength/colour of light, and the angle of incidence.
common_errors: wrote more than two factors
confused lateral displacement factor with thickness
wrong terms: colour/wavelength of prism instead of light
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Review and demonstrate all factors influencing each physical quantity repeatedly.

marking_schemes.question_text: Define Centre of Gravity.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: It is a point about which the (algebraic) sum of the moments of the molecular weights of the body is zero or implied/ It is a point through which the weight of the body acts (vertically downwards or towards the centre of the earth.) or implied.
key_points: Point where algebraic sum of moments of molecular weights is zero
Point through which weight of body acts vertically downwards
marking_schemes.model_answer: Centre of gravity is a point about which the algebraic sum of the moments of the weights of all the particles of the body is zero, i.e., the point through which the entire weight of the body appears to act vertically downwards.
common_errors: incomplete definitions missing keywords 'point', 'moment of weights', 'sum of moments is zero'
wrote sum of weights/masses is zero instead of sum of moments
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss concept of moments produced by molecular weights with diagrammatic representation.

marking_schemes.question_text: A hollow ice cream cone has height 6 cm. Where is the position of its centre of gravity from the broad base?
key_points: C.G. of hollow cone is at h/3 from base
marking_schemes.model_answer: For a hollow cone, C.G. is at h/3 from the base = 6/3 = 2 cm above the broad base.
common_errors: wrote h/3 without substituting value of h
erroneous answers like 6/4=1.5cm or 6/2=3cm
used general phrase 'at the centre' instead of precise value
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay special emphasis to centre of gravity of all regular bodies with specific numerical answers.

marking_schemes.question_text: A hollow ice cream cone has height 6 cm. Will its position change when it is filled completely with honey? Write Yes or No.
key_points: Filling with honey changes mass distribution (more mass near base), shifting C.G.
common_errors: unclear that C.G. depends on distribution of mass
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss with examples that C.G. depends on distribution of mass; in cone more mass is towards base when filled.

marking_schemes.question_text: Two identical marbles A and B are rolled down along Path 1 (frictionless) and Path 2 (rough) respectively. Which marble will surely reach the next peak?
key_points: Marble on frictionless path (A) retains all mechanical energy, reaching next peak
common_errors: could not comprehend question
no clarity on frictionless vs rough surfaces
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give more practice with application-based questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: Two identical marbles A and B are rolled down along Path 1 (frictionless) and Path 2 (rough) respectively. Along which path/s the mechanical energy will be conserved?
key_points: Mechanical energy conserved only in frictionless Path 1
common_errors: failed to recognise mechanical energy conserved only without friction
confused mechanical energy conservation with total energy conservation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss different forms of energy and law of conservation of energy as a whole.

marking_schemes.question_text: Two identical marbles A and B are rolled down along Path 1 (frictionless) and Path 2 (rough) respectively. Along which path/s is the law of conservation of energy obeyed?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Path 1 as well as Path 2/ both paths/1 and 2/A and B or implied.
key_points: Law of conservation of total energy is obeyed universally regardless of friction
common_errors: could not differentiate between conservation of mechanical energy and conservation of total energy
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay emphasis on critical distinction between mechanical energy conservation (needs frictionless) and total energy conservation (universal).

marking_schemes.question_text: Given are two pulleys. Copy and complete the labelled diagram connecting the two pulleys with a tackle to obtain Velocity Ratio = 2.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Correct connection of tackle. Labelling T and E correctly with directions.
key_points: Correct connection of pulley tackle for V.R.=2
Label tension (T) and effort (E) with correct directions
marking_schemes.model_answer: The two pulleys are connected with a string forming a tackle where the number of strands supporting the load equals 2 (V.R.=2), with tension T marked along the string and effort E marked in the convenient (downward) direction.
common_errors: tension direction not indicated
marked tension sections as T1,T2,T3
direction of effort not indicated
bulging tackle
no rigid support shown
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss intricacies in drawing diagram; give adequate practice; ask students to mark tension, effort and load.

marking_schemes.question_text: If Load = 48 kgf and efficiency is 80% then calculate Mechanical Advantage (V.R.=2).
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Efficiency = M.A./V.R. ∴ 80/100 = M.A./2 ∴ M.A. = 1.6 [Substitution is a must]
common_errors: kept answer as fraction 8/5 instead of decimal 1.6
wrote unnecessary unit for M.A.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Advise students to answer numericals in decimal form up to two decimal places.

marking_schemes.question_text: If Load = 48 kgf and efficiency is 80% then calculate Effort needed to lift the load.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: M.A. = L/E ∴ 1.6 = 48/E [Substitution in any form] ∴ E = 480/16 = 30 kgf /300N/294 N
common_errors: carried out calculation using ideal MA
calculation errors
units missing/confusion between kgf and N
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give adequate practice of numericals; emphasise correct answers with unit.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name the waves used in SONAR.
common_errors: wrote ultraviolet/infrared/radio waves instead of ultrasonic waves
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss the three types of mechanical waves: ultrasonic, infrasonic, sonic; distinguish from EM waves.

marking_schemes.question_text: Lata stands between two cliffs (Cliff A 170m away, Cliff B 160m away) and claps her hands. Determine the time taken by her to hear the first echo. Speed of sound in air 320 ms-1.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: v = 2d/t ∴ 320 = 2×160/t ∴ t = 320/320 = 1 s. If d=10 m is calculated and identified d<17 m and no echo is heard.
key_points: First echo heard from nearer cliff B (160m)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The first echo is heard from Cliff B, which is closer (160 m). Using v=2d/t: 320 = 2×160/t, so t = 1 s.
common_errors: erroneously considered distance as 10m (difference between cliffs)
unaware minimum 17m distance needed to hear echo
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give sufficient practice of numericals involving principle of echo; explain conditions of echo in detail.

marking_schemes.question_text: Complete the following radioactive reaction: X → Y + 2^4He → 91^234Z + -1^0e
marking_schemes.model_answer: ₉₂²³⁸X → ₉₀²³⁴Y + ₂⁴He (alpha emission); ₉₀²³⁴Y → ₉₁²³⁴Z + ₋₁⁰e (beta emission)
common_errors: confused by presentation of nuclear equation
difficulty with reverse calculation when more than one emission happened
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain that emitted particle cannot become reactant for next step; write reaction in two separate steps.

marking_schemes.question_text: Uranium is available in two forms U-235 and U-238. Which of the two isotopes of Uranium is more fissionable?
key_points: U-235 is more fissionable than U-238
common_errors: erroneously answered U-238
wrote both names
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise that U-235 is more fissionable of the two isotopes.

marking_schemes.question_text: In the given diagram, a vibrating tuning fork is kept near the mouth of a burette filled with water. At a length of 5 cm of the air column, a loud sound is heard. Name the phenomenon illustrated by the above experiment.
common_errors: erroneously wrote forced vibrations
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Tell students to mention all keywords while writing definitions.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why is a loud sound heard at this particular length (5 cm)?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Natural frequency of the tuning fork matched with the natural frequency of the air column and the amplitude of vibrations of air particles increased/Generalised statement can be accepted (Natural is must at any one place, frequency matching and increased amplitude is a must.)
key_points: Natural frequency of tuning fork matches natural frequency of air column
Amplitude of vibration of air particles increases, producing loud sound
marking_schemes.model_answer: At this length, the natural frequency of the air column matches the natural frequency of the tuning fork, causing resonance. This increases the amplitude of vibration of air particles, producing a loud sound.
common_errors: missing terms 'natural', 'matching' and 'amplitude'
confused frequency of the burette with air column
did not mention amplitude-loudness relation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Reinforce that length of vibrating air column is responsible for resonance; demonstrate practically.

marking_schemes.question_text: If the present tuning fork is replaced with a tuning fork of higher frequency, should the length of the air column increase or decrease to produce a loud sound? Give a reason.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Decrease. The frequency of vibrating air column is inversely proportional to the length of the air-column/ f ∝ 1/t.
key_points: Reason: frequency of air column is inversely proportional to its length
marking_schemes.model_answer: The length should decrease, because the frequency of the vibrating air column is inversely proportional to its length (f ∝ 1/l).
common_errors: missed writing correct reasoning
wrote 'length of water column' instead of 'air column'
wrote 'frequency of burette' instead of 'frequency of tuning fork'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain concept of factors affecting frequency and how it affects length; give rigorous application-level practice.

marking_schemes.question_text: The voltage-current readings of a certain material are shown: Voltage (10V,20V,30V) Current (2A,3A,4A). State whether the conductor used is ohmic or non-ohmic.
key_points: V/I ratio is not constant (5, 6.67, 7.5), hence non-ohmic
common_errors: determined answer solely by examining slope, ignoring that V-I graph must pass through origin
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ensure V-I graph passes through origin to confirm ohmic behaviour, even if slope appears constant.

marking_schemes.question_text: Justify your answer regarding whether the conductor is ohmic or non-ohmic.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Even though slope constant V:I ratio is not constant. ∴ The graph line will not pass through the origin. Graph (line) will not pass through the origin/ Resistance is not constant/ diagram VI graph not passing through origin/ V/I not constant or implied.
key_points: V/I ratio (resistance) is not constant across readings, so graph does not pass through origin
marking_schemes.model_answer: The ratio V/I is not constant (5, 6.67, 7.5 Ω), meaning resistance is not constant, so the V-I graph would not pass through the origin, indicating a non-ohmic conductor.
common_errors: only calculated slope and wrote ohmic conductor
calculated V:I ratio but wrote non-ohmic without proper explanation
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Ask students to verify whether straight line passes through origin even if slope seems constant.

marking_schemes.question_text: State Ohm's law.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Provided the physical condition/temperature of the conductor remains the same, current through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across the ends of the conductor.
key_points: Current is directly proportional to potential difference
marking_schemes.model_answer: Provided the physical conditions (temperature) of the conductor remain constant, the current flowing through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends.
common_errors: did not mention constant temperature
gave only mathematical relation instead of proper statement
wrote 'I directly proportional to R'
wrote 'I inversely proportional to V'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach statements and laws with proper terms and conditions; ask students to articulate complete statements.

marking_schemes.question_text: Below is the diagram of a transformer showing a primary coil with more turns and secondary coil with fewer turns. Identify the type of transformer.
key_points: Primary coil has more turns than secondary coil, making it a step-down transformer
common_errors: confused with wiring in diagram, misinterpreted as step-up transformer
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain transformer with schematic diagram; distinguish step-up and step-down transformers.

marking_schemes.question_text: In this type of transformer which of the wire is thicker, the primary or the secondary? Give a reason.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Secondary. As the current in the secondary coil increases/ to decrease the resistance/to minimise the loss of energy/ to prevent overheating of coil/ copper loss or implied.
key_points: Reason: current in secondary coil is higher, thicker wire reduces resistance and prevents overheating/copper loss
marking_schemes.model_answer: The secondary wire is thicker because the current in the secondary coil is higher (step-down transformer), and a thicker wire has less resistance, minimising energy loss due to overheating (copper loss).
common_errors: misinterpreted more turns as indicative of thickness, incorrectly identified primary as thicker
explained in terms of voltage instead of current
lack of understanding that more current needs less resistance
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Highlight disparity between step-up and step-down transformers based on voltage, current, turns and thickness relations.

marking_schemes.question_text: Study the diagram: two parallel branches, one with 10Ω and 6Ω in series (16Ω), other with 12Ω and 4Ω in series (16Ω), connected in parallel, with a 4V cell. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Each branch has resistance 16Ω (10+6 and 12+4). In parallel: R = (16×16)/(16+16) = 8Ω
common_errors: incorrect units
mathematical errors e.g. 1/16+1/16=1/8=8Ω
incorrect formula or substitution
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Sufficient practice of numericals involving combination of resistors; insist on writing correct answers with units.

marking_schemes.question_text: Calculate the current drawn from the cell.
common_errors: missed unit
error carried from previous part
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay emphasis on including units in numerical answers.

marking_schemes.question_text: State whether the current through 10 Ω resistor is greater than, less than or equal to the current through the 12 Ω resistor.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Current through both the resistors is the same.
key_points: Both branches have equal resistance (16Ω each), so current splits equally
marking_schemes.model_answer: The current through the 10Ω resistor is equal to the current through the 12Ω resistor, since both branches (10+6Ω and 12+4Ω) have the same total resistance of 16Ω.
common_errors: went into tedious calculations reaching erroneous answer
did not realise current splits equally since both branch resistances are equal
substituted V=4V, R=10Ω incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Elucidate that in a parallel circuit, current is inversely proportional to total resistance of that branch.

marking_schemes.question_text: 85 g of water at 30°C is cooled to 5°C by adding certain mass of ice. Find the mass of ice required. [Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 Jg-1°C-1, Specific latent heat of fusion = 336 Jg-1]
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (By principle of mixtures Heat lost = heat gained) m∆w×sw = (ml + m∆s)ice. ∴ 85 × 4.2 × (30-5) = m×336 + m×4.2×5 ∴ 85×4.2×25 = 4.2×m(80+5) ∴ 85×25 = m×85 ∴ m = 25
key_points: Heat lost by water = Heat gained by ice (in melting and warming to 5°C)
marking_schemes.model_answer: Heat lost by water = Heat gained by ice: 85×4.2×25 = m×336 + m×4.2×5. Solving, m = 25 g
common_errors: did not attempt question
substitution error - only considered ml for melting ice, not mcΔt for warming to final temperature
calculation errors
unit errors
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give more practice of numericals of different types involving heat exchange; advise constructing equation using heating curve.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why does it become pleasantly warm when the lakes start freezing?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Large quantity of heat/ latent heat of fusion/ latent heat/ 336 J/g or value or value in other units/ is given out/ liberated/ released (in the atmosphere) or implied.
key_points: Large quantity of latent heat of fusion is released to surroundings during freezing
marking_schemes.model_answer: When water freezes into ice, a large amount of latent heat of fusion is released into the surroundings, making it feel pleasantly warm.
common_errors: confused release of heat during freezing with absorption during melting
missed mentioning 'large' amount of heat
wrote specific heat capacity instead of latent heat
vague/incorrect answers
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain that heat is released during freezing and absorbed during melting; underline keywords in reasoning questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: Water freezes to form ice. What change would you expect in the average kinetic energy of the molecules?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (There is) no change (in the average kinetic energy of the molecules.) or implied.
key_points: Average kinetic energy remains constant during change of state (only temperature-dependent)
marking_schemes.model_answer: There is no change in the average kinetic energy of the molecules, as it remains constant during a change of state.
common_errors: most answered increases or decreases due to lack of concept clarity
did not recall kinetic energy remains constant during phase change
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain what happens to kinetic and potential energy during phase change; temperature and average KE remain constant during change of state.

marking_schemes.question_text: Which will contain more heat energy 1 g of ice at 0°C or 1 g water at 0°C?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: 1 g of water at 0 0C (contains more heat energy than 1 g of ice at 0 0C).
key_points: Water at 0°C has more heat energy than ice at 0°C due to latent heat content
marking_schemes.model_answer: 1 g of water at 0°C contains more heat energy than 1 g of ice at 0°C.
common_errors: few answered as ice due to careless error
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify misconception: at same temperature, heat energy content of water is higher than ice due to latent heat.

marking_schemes.question_text: State one factor that affects the magnitude of induced current in an AC generator.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Induced current depends on is directly proportional to: The strength of the magnetic field; The number of turns of the coil; The area of the coil; The speed of rotation of the coil; Rate of change of magnetic flux. [Any one factor.]
key_points: Any one of: strength of magnetic field, number of turns, area of coil, speed of rotation, rate of change of magnetic flux
marking_schemes.model_answer: The magnitude of induced current in an AC generator is directly proportional to the speed of rotation of the coil (or any one of: strength of magnetic field, number of turns, area of coil).
common_errors: confused with factors affecting speed of rotation of DC motor
gave more than required factors, some incorrect
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain a.c. generator with diagram in detail; distinguish between DC motor and AC generator factors.

marking_schemes.question_text: ABCD is a cardboard kept perpendicular to conductor XY with a magnetic compass at point P, showing positions P1 and P2 before and after current flow. Name the rule that is used to predict the direction of deflection of the magnetic compass.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Right hand thumb rule/ Amphere's swimming rule/maxwell's cork screw rule/SNOW rule/Right-hand grip rule/ Right hand palm rule.
key_points: Right hand thumb rule (or equivalent: Ampere's swimming rule, Maxwell's corkscrew rule, SNOW rule)
common_errors: incorrect answers like Fleming's left/right-hand rule, Ampere's right-hand rule, clock rule
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Emphasise application of these rules and clarify which physical quantity each rule identifies.

marking_schemes.question_text: State the direction of current in the conductor (X to Y or Y to X) when the circuit is complete.
key_points: Current direction is from X to Y as determined by compass deflection and right hand thumb rule
common_errors: found it difficult to comprehend the diagram
guesswork used by many
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain that magnetic needle deflects in the direction of the magnetic field around the conductor.

marking_schemes.question_text: If resistance R is increased, then what will be the effect on the magnetic lines of force around the conductor?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The number of lines of force will decrease/ less crowded/ spaced out/ less dense or implied.
key_points: Increasing R decreases current, decreasing number/density of magnetic lines of force
marking_schemes.model_answer: Increasing resistance R decreases the current, so the magnetic lines of force around the conductor become less crowded (fewer in number/less dense).
common_errors: errors carried from confusion in previous part
unable to understand concept correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain how change in resistance affects current and thereby strength of magnetic field; give practical demonstration.
